title: SynchronizationContext
sub: Who runs the code after await
cards/0/body:
await remembers the current SynchronizationContext. In WPF and WinForms that means "the UI thread": the continuation is queued to the window and runs there, so you can touch controls.

A console app or ASP.NET Core has no context: any pool thread runs the continuation.
cards/1/task: Run the scenario in WPF, then switch to a console app and see who runs the continuations.
cards/2/q: Why can you write label.Text = … after await in WPF?
cards/2/options/0: The continuation came back to the UI thread through the synchronization context
cards/2/options/1: WPF lets you change controls from any thread
cards/2/explain: That's the main job of SynchronizationContext in windowed apps.
cards/3/q: Where is there a SynchronizationContext by default? Select all that apply.
cards/3/explain: A console app and ASP.NET Core have no context; the pool runs continuations.
cards/4/body:
The UI context is a queue: clicks, redraws, continuations after await. One thread works through it, one item at a time.

If that thread is busy or blocked, the queue stalls.
cards/5/q: The UI thread is busy with a long computation while a continuation waits in the queue. When does it run?
cards/5/options/0: When the thread frees up and reaches it
cards/5/explain: The continuation waits its turn, just like clicks.
cards/6/body: If no SynchronizationContext is set, await looks at the current TaskScheduler. By default that's the thread pool.
cards/6/deep: SynchronizationContext.Current and TaskScheduler.Current are checked at the moment of the await. You install your own context with SynchronizationContext.SetSynchronizationContext; that's how test frameworks and Unity run continuations on a single thread.
